newsitem.title: USA: US 10-yr note seen boosted by Treasury supply cut.
newsitem.headline: US 10-yr note seen boosted by Treasury supply cut.

text.p: U.S. 10-year note prices are likely to rise in the short term, as supply looks to shrink after a Treasury decision on Monday to eliminate two 10-year auctions, analysts said.

But the expected boost is likely to be short-lived since an expected increase in corporate debt supply is seen offsetting the reduction in the availability of longer-term federal debt issuances, they added.

"Initially, the knee jerk reaction will be to drive them up," said Chris Fitzmaurice, a 10-year trader at Salomon Brothers. "But just because there will be less auctions doesn't mean there will be an enormous reduction in supply."
The Treasury on Monday announced that it was eliminating the July and October conventional 10-year note auctions.
In addition, Treasury will offer a five-year inflation-index-linked note in July, sell a new 10-year index-linked note in January, 1998 and issue a 30-year index-linked bond sometime next year.
Treasuries, which had been as much as 3/8-point lower, barely budged on the announcement.
Traders said the muted response was because the market had anticipated the Treasury's announcement for some time, and it was already factored into the market last last week as speculation increased.

"In the near term, (the cutting of auctions) will make the 10-year note sector more (expensive), probably by a few basis points," said Elliott Platt, director of economic reserach at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
"There has been enough speculation about this that maybe it will not be a market factor," he added.
Platt stressed he did not see the index linked notes as replacing the now-cut 10-year notes.
One head trader at a European primary dealership said that once the market gets adjusted to the new schedule, the imapct will be minimal.
Until then, he added, the yield curve between two-year and 10-year notes should flatten, while the spread between 10-year notes and 30-year bonds should widen.
"Clearly, there is demand for 10-year notes," the trader said.
Indeed, volume in 10-year notes was very high over the past few sessions.
At Monday afternoon, 10-year note volume was some $4.0 billion, according to GovPX, in an otherwise average volume session.

Further, 10-year issues trade "special" in the repo market at about 4.50 to 4.75 percent. Financing for the old 10-year note was an even tighter 1.5 percent and had been as low as 0.60 percent earlier on Monday.
"The market is rich up here," said Fitzmaurice. "It's probably a good selling opportunity for 10-years.

"Fundamentals will take time to overwhelm the technical factors" of the fewer auctions, said another trader. "So, does it worry me? No. The net of it is that it will have an impact only in the short term."

Others pointed out that the effects of adding the two extra 10-year note auctions in early 1996 were negligible because when the Treasury moved from four to six regular 10-year auctions, the sizes of each sale were reduced.
In 1994, 10-year note auctions were around $12.0 billion, rising to $13.5 billion by the end of 1995.
And the first two 10-year note sales of 1996 were $14.0 billion, before the Treasury cut the size to $10.0 billion for the next four auctions.
The two 10-year auctions in 1997 were $12.0 billion each, while the size of the 10-year inflation protected notes were $7.0 billion in January and $8.0 billion in April.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, in a news conference on Monday, said the Treasury was able to cut the two extra 10-year note auctions because of progress in cutting the budget deficit and success of the indexed-linked issues.
Eliminating the notes was proposed earlier in the year by the PSA The Bond Market Trade Association.
Platt said he did not think it was necessary to cut the two auctions, and Treasury instead could have continued cutting the sizes of other issues.
In recent months, Treasury drasticallly slashed the size of bills and reduced the size of coupons.
Critics of the continued cutting of auction sizes said that it reduces volatility and drives up prices, evidenced by what was described as a very expensive 4.93 percent rate on three-month T-bills.
Since the beginning of the year, Treasury has cut the three- and six-month bills to $14.0 billion from $28.0 billion.
Traders said there has been virtually no activity in the bills in months, since those who have the bills are not parting with them.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
